## I've got data. Why is reuse still so hard? {#framing-the-challenge}

You have a biological question, some promising files and a deadline. Before you can analyse anything, you need to find the right columns, connect them to the methods and work out what can be compared. The answers may be scattered across papers, appendices and emails. New questions appear when you combine the tables.

Later, you may be the person asked to publish the data behind a paper or make them [FAIR](glossary.html#fair). Reconstructing those explanations at the end takes more work, and the next user may still need to email you. Capturing the answers as you go can help both of you.

Our example question is to **assemble the best available annual estimates of salmon spawner abundance by Conservation Unit (CU)** across several regions. A CU groups salmon populations for conservation and assessment. We want records for each CU and year, with differences in scope, method and uncertainty kept visible.

The diagram follows that project from finding data to publishing them. The left route begins with files and scattered explanations. The right shows how the work could change when those explanations travel with reviewed [Salmon Data Packages](glossary.html#salmon-data-package). **Next** adds a phase to both timelines; select a step to explore its detail.

<section id="salmon-workflow-guided" aria-label="Interactive workflow comparison">
<p>The interactive comparison requires JavaScript. The text version below follows the same four phases.</p>
</section>

[Open the diagram on its own](files/workflow-explorer/index.html).

<details class="workflow-text" id="workflow-text">
<summary>Read the workflow as text</summary>

1. **Find and understand the data.** Starting with separate files can mean searching papers and asking providers what columns represent. A reviewed package keeps the data, descriptions, methods and evidence together. Preparing one from raw files begins with a drawing, dictionary and human review.
2. **Check and combine the estimates.** In the usual route, reshaping and combining tables can expose questions that send us back to the sources. With common formats and explicit meanings, we can write repeatable mappings and retain the decisions. A person still checks whether the estimates fit the question.
3. **Draw a conclusion the evidence supports.** In our teaching example, reading a status-confidence rating as abundance precision would produce an unsupported claim. Checking the definition catches that mistake. The green check represents this checked interpretation.
4. **Publish once, help the next project.** Rebuilding metadata at the end repeats work. A package preserves the explanations for validation and publication, with source credit and processing history. Later users can reuse the package and its maintained terms.

[Static overview of the interpretation loop](fig/comparison-workflows.svg).

</details>

The Yukon and Fraser sources below make the diagram concrete: `mean` and `SpnForAbd_Total` are candidate abundance fields, while their uncertainty descriptions require a closer look. Central Coast adds a further question about moving from stream records to CU estimates.

## The archetypical data problem

These are small excerpts from the sources suggested for this comparison. The original field names and values are preserved; the tables show selected columns. The linked CSV excerpts retain all source columns for these records. They are an introductory comparison, separate from the NuSEDS dataset we will use for the exercises. [Source notes and selection](files/intro-comparison/PROVENANCE.txt) and a [checksum manifest](files/intro-comparison/source-manifest.json) accompany them.

### Yukon Chinook reconstruction

The [Yukon project](https://github.com/Pacific-salmon-assess/Yukon-Chinook-CU-reconstructions/blob/3390d4f2a706e1923785aef24e96eba17a7002c0/README.md) reconstructs CU time series using border-passage estimates, genetic information and reconstructed harvest rates. Its output has a column called `mean`.

| stock | year | mean |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| NorthernYukonR.andtribs. | 2022 | 504.605427825807 |
| NorthernYukonR.andtribs. | 2023 | 2009.4529003227 |

[Open the Yukon excerpt](files/intro-comparison/yukon-excerpt.csv). The same records also contain `lower`, `upper` and `cv`. A number headed `mean` needs its methods context before we can tell what was estimated and how its uncertainty is described.

### Fraser Rapid Status Assessment

The [Rapid Status output](https://github.com/sos-program/Approved-WSP-Statuses/blob/05643cf7474e2c468e21e30edbf1da0ef9a060a8/OUTPUT/README.md) covers multiple CUs. Here we have selected one Lower Fraser Chinook CU. Its abundance fields sit alongside status metrics and decision-tree outputs.

| CU_ID | Stock | Year | SpnForAbd_Total |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| CK-03 | Lower Fraser River_FA_0.3 | 2022 | 82859 |
| CK-03 | Lower Fraser River_FA_0.3 | 2023 | 146371 |

[Open the Fraser excerpt](files/intro-comparison/fraser-excerpt.csv). Its other columns include `SpnForAbd_Wild`, `DataType`, `ConfidenceRating`, `RelUBM` and `BinPath`. Some describe abundance, some describe assessment metrics, and some describe how a status was assigned.

### What do those columns actually mean?

The Fraser output has a [field dictionary](https://github.com/sos-program/Approved-WSP-Statuses/blob/05643cf7474e2c468e21e30edbf1da0ef9a060a8/OUTPUT/README.md). It describes `SpnForAbd_Total` as total spawner abundance used for abundance-based assessment metrics, and distinguishes it from wild spawner abundance. It also distinguishes an absolute abundance series from a relative index through `DataType`. The displayed rows use `Abs_Abd`; another CU's series may have a different basis.

The Yukon [methods description](https://github.com/Pacific-salmon-assess/Yukon-Chinook-CU-reconstructions/blob/3390d4f2a706e1923785aef24e96eba17a7002c0/README.md) places its estimates within a run reconstruction. That supports treating `mean` as a candidate abundance estimate, while the included fish, stock-to-CU correspondence and uncertainty definition still need to be checked for our purpose. The project also explains that historical estimates can change when the model is updated.

**Uncertainty about an abundance estimate and confidence in an assessment status describe different things.** In the 2023 Yukon row, `lower` is `1139.14176352581` and `upper` is `2879.76403711959`; we would check the interval's definition in the methods. In the 2023 Fraser row, `ConfidenceRating` is `High`; the dictionary says this is confidence in the **status**. We cannot use that rating as an abundance interval.

This is the warning/check comparison in **Phase 3**. Imagine concluding that the Fraser abundance estimate is more precise because its record says `High`. That conclusion does not follow from the field's definition. The checked interpretation keeps status confidence separate from uncertainty about the abundance estimate. This is an illustrative mistake using real fields, not an error attributed to either source's authors.

For our question, different methods may be acceptable if we retain their context and assess their suitability. A study designed to compare one estimation method would need a tighter selection. These rows concern different CUs; we would retain each CU's records in a combined table, rather than join them as observations of the same population.

## My life would have been easier if the meanings came with the data

A [Salmon Data Package (SDP)](glossary.html#salmon-data-package) keeps data together with descriptions, code meanings and source information. Links to maintained [controlled-vocabulary](glossary.html#controlled-vocabulary) and [ontology](glossary.html#ontology) terms can make its meanings easier to find and relate across datasets.

Here is a **prepared description preview** for the two candidate fields. It illustrates what we would record; the comparison still needs source and domain review before accepting a mapping.

| Part of the description | Yukon `mean` | Fraser `SpnForAbd_Total` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quantity to investigate | Estimated spawner abundance from the reconstruction | Total spawner abundance used for abundance-based metrics |
| Entity and time | Source `stock` label and `year`; verify the CU identifier correspondence and year definition | `CU_ID`, `Stock` and escapement `Year` |
| Scope and scale | Check included fish and coverage of the reconstructed CU estimate | Check total versus wild scope and `DataType` for the selected CU |
| Method and uncertainty | Retain the reconstruction reference and the meaning of `lower`, `upper` and `cv` | Follow the CU's data-preparation narrative; retain status confidence separately |
| Shared meaning | Compare the abundance property with a shared definition | Compare the abundance property with the same definition; preserve the different qualifiers |

For example, the Salmon Domain Ontology's [Abundance definition](https://github.com/salmon-data-mobilization/salmon-domain-ontology/blob/d45f8f7cc857d92af8bbe54a7c89b2a4a14784b2/ontology/modules/02-observation-measurement.ttl) can help describe the **property** of interest. The complete variable also needs its entity and qualifiers. Sharing that property would not make the Yukon stock and Fraser CU the same population, or establish that every estimate is interchangeable.

This prepared description is the work carried forward on the diagram's right-hand route. **Phase 1** keeps the explanation with each source. **Phase 2** uses it to find candidate fields and assess their fit. **Phase 3** catches the confidence mistake. By **Phase 4**, those explanations are already available for publication and the next user.

The R package `metasalmon` and its Python counterpart help build, review, validate and prepare these packages for publication. Study-specific integration code uses the recorded mappings; people resolve unsupported meanings and decide which differences matter. A common structure makes the work easier to repeat and inspect.

### Reuse meanings, and develop the ones that are missing

A maintained term has a stable identifier, or [IRI](glossary.html#iri), that can be linked from the metadata. Reusing it connects our description to its published definition. When an organization's meaning is more specific, a local vocabulary or ontology can preserve that definition and a [bridge](glossary.html#bridge) can state how it relates to shared terms.

When a reusable concept is missing, we can prepare a [term request](glossary.html#term-request) with a definition, examples and supporting evidence for the Salmon Domain Ontology's stewards. Those terms and mappings need their own review and release. Publishing them lets later data packages reuse the work, alongside the separate process of publishing data to a catalog.

## And now someone sends you a third dataset

Now imagine adding Central Coast NuSEDS stream records. The [Central Coast estimation example](https://salmonwatersheds.ca/document/lib_451/) uses additional information and an expansion approach to produce CU-level estimates. A stream record and an estimate for a whole CU can concern salmon abundance while covering different entities and spatial scales.

This brings us back to **Phases 1–2**: which records belong to the CU, what observations cover it, how are repeated or missing records handled, and what expansion method is used? An ontology link describes meaning; it does not provide an expansion factor or perform the calculation.

We will practise making those relationships explicit with the **Fraser Coho NuSEDS teaching slice** below. It is a different regional example from the Central Coast illustration. Our first task is to draw what its records describe and write a dictionary, so we can see what is known and what still needs evidence before using packaging software or AI.

## Let's make one dataset easier for the next person

Download and extract the [Fraser Coho workshop kit](files/fraser-coho-workshop.zip). The hands-on chapters use the **173-row, 14-column NuSEDS Fraser Coho 2023–2024 slice** in `raw_data/nuseds-fraser-coho-2023-2024.csv`. Open a copy in a spreadsheet, or follow the displayed table, keeping the source unchanged.

It comes from Fisheries and Oceans Canada's Fraser and BC Interior NuSEDS workbook on the [Government of Canada's Open Government Portal](https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/c48669a3-045b-400d-b730-48aafe8c5ee6). The kit preserves provenance and the [official DFO dictionary](files/fraser-coho-workshop/raw_data/official-nuseds-dictionary.csv). That dictionary was retrieved on 8 September 2026 and may postdate the source workbook.

Here are the first three records, showing our six focus columns. The blank estimate is also blank in the source.

| POP_<wbr>ID | WATERBODY | ANALYSIS_<wbr>YR | SPECIES | NATURAL_<wbr>ADULT_<wbr>SPAWNERS | ESTIMATE_<wbr>METHOD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 46200 | BONAPARTE RIVER | 2023 | Coho | 758 | Resistivity Counter |
| 44965 | CLAPPERTON CREEK | 2023 | Coho |  | Not Applicable |
| 46190 | COLDWATER RIVER | 2023 | Coho | 7943 | Combined Methods |

We will describe these six fields and review supplied descriptions for the other eight, asking which fish were included and how each method produced its result.

The table has **164 distinct population–analysis-year pairs across 173 rows**, so population plus year does not uniquely identify a row. It has no CU field. A CU comparison would therefore need additional evidence connecting these population records to CUs.

The compound name `NATURAL_ADULT_SPAWNERS` makes the interpretation problem concrete. The [entity](glossary.html#entity) is what the data concerns; its [property](glossary.html#property) is the characteristic of interest, such as abundance. The full [variable](glossary.html#variable) also depends on scope and context. We will investigate “adult” and “natural”, the year basis, unit and method, keeping unsupported interpretations as questions.

## Give the next user a better starting point

The first estimate, `758`, will follow this route:

**Draw the relationships → describe and decompose the dictionary → peer review → build the package → assess term and AI suggestions → validate and prepare publication.**

[Chapter 2](session-2.html) starts with the drawing. [Chapter 3](session-3.html) separates the entity, abundance property, result and unit from scope, year and method; “natural” remains a source question. [Chapters 4–7](session-4.html) translate the reviewed explanation into a package, review suggestions and preview publication. The [teaching-record page](reference.html#teaching-record) records the catalog's actual status.

[Chapters 8–12](session-8.html) return to meanings that need stewardship: a local vocabulary or model, a bridge, or a shared-term request. After review and release, later data packages can link to those maintained terms. The optional [worked illustration](fig/record-to-reuse.svg) follows the same estimate through the stages.

## What you'll take away from the two days

Day 1 is a six-hour beginner route to a described package and test catalog publication. Day 2 adds six hours of vocabulary, ontology and contribution work. Together, they support:

- **Reusable data publication:** make the data and their descriptions discoverable and usable.
- **Shared terminology:** reuse maintained terms and propose new ones when a reusable concept is missing.
- **Local stewardship:** maintain specific meanings and connect them to shared definitions through explicit bridges.

The same diagram and dictionary support all three. The [Day 2 guide](advanced.html) introduces the [SKOS](glossary.html#skos) vocabulary, [OWL](glossary.html#owl) model, bridge and contribution exercises in the extracted kit's `semantic-lab/` folder; [setup](index.html#download-and-open-the-workshop-kit) explains where to find it. The [outcomes illustration](fig/outcomes-overview.svg) shows how the three outputs connect.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: challenge

## Activity: Describe what the next user would need

Return to the Fraser Coho table with a partner. Spend 15 minutes, including sharing your example, identifying one question you could answer from the table and one that needs more evidence.

Write three short notes:

- The field or value that raises your question.
- The description, relationship or source evidence that would help someone else interpret it.
- The workshop stage where you expect to prepare or review that information.

Keep these notes for the diagram and dictionary exercises. Consider how publishing a clear explanation now would change the work of someone who finds the data later.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: keypoints

- Different column names can refer to a related quantity; scope, scale, method, year and uncertainty still affect whether estimates fit an analysis.
- A reviewed package records the interpretation work, and shared terms connect its meanings to maintained definitions.
- The Yukon and Fraser excerpts frame the comparison; the same 173-row, 14-column Fraser Coho slice supports the hands-on chapters.
- We draw, describe and peer-review the NuSEDS dataset before using metasalmon or AI.
- Publishing data, developing local meanings and contributing shared terms are connected parts of making the next person's work easier.
